script.text: On Tuesday, a section of the bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea fell into the sea, footage geolocated by CNN shows. Ukraine has struck this bridge before. So why does this one bridge matter so much?

For Moscow, it is a supply line and a symbol. For Kyiv, it is a target. What is this bridge, and why was it built? Why does it matter for the war in the south? And what can Russia do now? Plus the open question: can it even be rebuilt while the war goes on?

Start with the map. Crimea is a peninsula in the Black Sea. In the east, a narrow strait separates it from Russia's Krasnodar region. That is the Kerch Strait. It connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. In 2014, Russia annexed Crimea. The U.N. General Assembly called the referendum behind it invalid, and most countries still see Crimea as part of Ukraine. Crimea is also home to Sevastopol, the main base of Russia's Black Sea Fleet. Back then, Crimea had no land connection to Russia. Supplies came by ferry, or overland through Ukraine. So Moscow built a crossing. Two bridges, in fact, side by side: one for cars and trucks, one for trains. It cost about two hundred and twenty-eight billion roubles, roughly three point seven billion dollars. In May 2018, Vladimir Putin opened the road bridge himself, driving a truck at the head of a convoy. Passenger trains followed at the end of 2019. For the Kremlin, the bridge became a symbol: Crimea, tied to Russia by steel and concrete. In the middle of the strait, two steel arches rise over the shipping channel, so ships can pass between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Remember those arches. Ukraine now says one of them has been destroyed. If you want one of these explainers every Wednesday, subscribing is how you get it.

So why would Ukraine want this bridge down? Follow the supplies. Since 2022, Russian forces have held a strip of southern Ukraine that links Russia to Crimea by land. In November 2022, Ukraine retook the city of Kherson, and Russian troops pulled back across the Dnipro river. Since then, the Dnipro river has formed the front line in Kherson region. The Institute for the Study of War calls the bridge one of two ground supply routes for Russia's southern forces. The other is the M-fourteen highway, through occupied Ukrainian territory. Reuters, quoted by Time, describes the bridge as the only direct link between Russia's transport network and the peninsula. Ukraine's General Staff calls the bridge a main artery for fuel, ammunition, equipment and personnel. That is the military side. There is also an economic one. Every ship sailing between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea passes under the bridge's arches. Russian ports like Rostov-on-Don and Taganrog sit on that sea, and grain leaves through this channel. Quick question: how long is the Kerch Bridge? Take a guess. About nineteen kilometres. That makes it the longest bridge in Europe. A long bridge has many spans, and every span is a possible weak point. What does it mean for you? Crimea is one of the hinges of this war. Who can move fuel and ammunition there shapes the front in the south, and with it, the talks about ending the war. Next: the attacks.

Ukraine has gone after this bridge before. Three attacks stand out. October eighth, 2022. An explosion on the road bridge. Russian authorities said a truck bomb went off, and fuel tanks on a passing train caught fire. Two road spans collapsed. Putin called it a terrorist act by Ukrainian special services. Ukraine did not claim it at the time. A day later, cars were crossing again on the lanes that still stood. July seventeenth, 2023. Two sea drones exploded under the bridge. Russia's anti-terror committee blamed Ukraine, and Ukraine's security service, the S.B.U., later said each drone carried eight hundred and fifty kilograms of explosives. A road span was destroyed. June third, 2025. The S.B.U. said it set off more than a tonne of explosives under water, against the bridge's supports. Look at the pattern. Each attack used a different method: a truck, sea drones, underwater charges. In 2022 and 2023, Russia repaired the damage and kept the crossing in use. After the 2025 attack, Russia reported no serious damage. Newsweek notes there was no confirmed Ukrainian attack on the bridge after June 2025, for almost eighteen months. That is what makes this week different.

Now, this week. On the nights of November sixteenth and seventeenth, Ukraine struck the bridge again, with drones and missiles, according to reports. This time, a section fell. The Institute for the Study of War says the road sections were wrecked. Footage geolocated by CNN and NBC News shows one road span collapsed into the water, while the rail bridge next to it appeared to still be standing. Ukraine's S.B.U. said a steel arch and the road span beneath it were destroyed, and the rail section was damaged. Russia's Transport Ministry halted all road and rail traffic. The business daily Vedomosti reported that trains were running again on one track, while repairs went on. Russia's Investigative Committee opened a terrorism case. Crimea's Russian-installed head, Sergei Aksyonov, said a drone killed two people in a district near the bridge. The Transport Ministry said no one was hurt on the bridge itself. President Zelensky called it an unprecedented operation, a response to Russian attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure. He said it was the seventh stage of an operation that ran for weeks. By Moscow's count, the scale was a record too. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed one thousand four hundred and forty-one Ukrainian drones in one night. The night before, it had claimed one thousand three hundred and thirty-six. Those numbers come from Moscow and could not be independently checked. Bridges were hit in Ukraine too. In Kyiv, missiles and drones struck the North and South bridges over the Dnipro, killing at least two people, officials said. And the timing: on Thursday, Putin meets Trump and Xi in Shenzhen, China. A Russian lawmaker, quoted by The War Zone, called the strikes propaganda timed for that summit. Kyiv has not commented on the timing.

What happens next? This week's reporting points to two paths. First, repair. Russian officials acknowledged the damage and vowed to fix it. After the attacks in 2022 and 2023, Russia repaired the damaged spans and reopened the road. This time, a whole road span lies in the water, and the reports we reviewed give no timeline for a repair. Second, other routes. An analyst quoted by Time says Russia can still use the land corridor and ferries, but they are slower, less efficient and more exposed to attack. The Institute for the Study of War expects Russian forces to lean more on the ground route between occupied Kherson region and Crimea, and says that complicates Russian logistics. And the arches matter beyond the front: every ship between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea passes under them. So, can the bridge be rebuilt while the war goes on? Moscow says yes. When, it has not said. Will cars drive across the Kerch road bridge again before the end of 2027? Tell us below: yes or no.
Russia answers with strikes on Ukraine's power grid. Why the grid keeps getting hit, and how much of it is left, is the video to watch next.

upload.description:
Why does Ukraine keep attacking the Kerch Bridge (Crimean Bridge), and why did this week's strike drop a road span into the sea? This explainer covers why Russia built the 19 km road and rail bridge to occupied Crimea after 2014, why it matters as a supply route for Russian forces in southern Ukraine and for shipping from the Sea of Azov, the earlier attacks in 2022, 2023 and 2025, what happened on November 16-17, 2026, and the paths now reported: repair or other routes. Claims by either side are attributed; figures that could not be verified are labelled.
